arXiv:2609.02882v2 [math.NT] 08 Sep 2026

A new proof that more than 2/32/3 of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are simple and on the critical line

Youness Lamzouri Address: Université de Lorraine, CNRS, IECL, F-54000 Nancy, France Email address: youness.lamzouri@univ-lorraine.fr
Date: September 8, 2026
Abstract.

We obtain a new, conceptually simpler, unconditional proof that more than 67.25%67.25\% of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are simple and on the critical line, and that at least 83.62%83.62\% of the non-trivial zeros are distinct. Our approach also yields two new unconditional estimates on simple zeros and zeros on the critical line. More precisely, we prove that the proportion of zeros that are simple or lie on the critical line (or both) is at least 88.76%88.76\%, and that the average of the proportions of simple zeros and of zeros on the critical line is at least 83.62%83.62\%. A proof of the bounds for simple zeros on the critical line and for distinct zeros was very recently produced by an internal research version of Claude developed by Anthropic and subsequently verified by two mathematicians at Anthropic, Levent Alpöge and Ralph Furman, whereas our two additional estimates are neither stated nor proved in the Claude paper. The argument produced by Claude is technically intricate, and its main mechanism is not immediately transparent. It combines several ingredients from linear algebra, including a finite-dimensional matrix representation of Weil’s Hermitian form and a rank–trace inequality for Hermitian matrices, with a second moment calculation over the zeros using the explicit formula. Our new approach proceeds by replacing the entire finite-dimensional matrix framework by a single Hilbert space inequality, which allows for a direct application of Montgomery’s theorem on the pair correlation of zeros of the zeta function, in the unconditional form obtained by Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 11M06, 11M26

1. Introduction

The Riemann hypothesis (RH) is one of the central open problems in mathematics and one of the seven Millennium Prize problems. This conjecture, which was formulated by Riemann in 1859, asserts that all the non-trivial zeros11 1 That is, the zeros lying in the critical strip 0⩽Re​(s)⩽10\leqslant\textup{Re}(s)\leqslant 1. of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line Re​(s)=1/2\textup{Re}(s)=1/2. Its truth would have tremendous applications in number theory, most notably for our understanding of the distribution of prime numbers.

Let ρ=β+i​γ\rho=\beta+i\gamma denote a non-trivial zero of the Riemann zeta function, and let mρm_{\rho} be its multiplicity. We write

N⁡(T):=∑ρ0<γ⩽T1,N(T):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\end{subarray}}1,

where the zeros are counted with multiplicity. The classical Riemann–von Mangoldt formula gives N⁡(T)∼T2​π​log⁡T,N(T)\sim\frac{T}{2\pi}\log T, as T→∞T\to\infty. In the absence of a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a fundamental problem has been to determine what proportion of the zeros can be shown to lie on the critical line. The first progress in this direction goes back to Hardy [15], who proved in 1914 that infinitely many zeros lie on the line Re​(s)=1/2\textup{Re}(s)=1/2. Hardy and Littlewood [16] subsequently showed that the number of such zeros up to height TT is ≫T\gg T. A fundamental breakthrough was made by Selberg [22], who pioneered the use of mollification in this problem and proved in 1942 that a positive proportion of the zeros lie on the critical line. In 1974, Levinson [18] introduced a new mollifier method and used it to prove that more than one third of the zeros lie on the line Re​(s)=1/2\textup{Re}(s)=1/2. Conrey [8] later developed Levinson’s method further and proved in 1989 that more than 2/52/5 of the zeros are simple and lie on the critical line. More recently, Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler [21] obtained the slightly better bounds

lim infT→∞N0​(T)N⁡(T)⩾0.417293andlim infT→∞N0s​(T)N⁡(T)⩾0.407511,\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{0}(T)}{N(T)}\geqslant 0.417293\qquad\text{and}\qquad\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{0}^{\textup{s}}(T)}{N(T)}\geqslant 0.407511,

where

N0(T):=∑ρ0<γ⩽Tβ=1/21andN0s(T):=|{ρ:0<γ⩽T,β=12,and mρ=1}|,N_{0}(T):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\\ \beta=1/2\end{subarray}}1\qquad\textup{and}\qquad N_{0}^{\textup{s}}(T):=\left|\left\{\rho:0<\gamma\leqslant T,\ \beta=\frac{1}{2},\ \text{and }m_{\rho}=1\right\}\right|,

and where the zeros in the definition of N0​(T)N_{0}(T) are counted with multiplicity. We also let

Ns(T):=∑ρ0<γ⩽Tmρ=11,Ns∪0(T):=∑ρ0<γ⩽Tmρ=1​or​β=1/21, and Nd(T):=|{ρ:0<γ⩽T}|.N_{s}(T):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\\ m_{\rho}=1\end{subarray}}1,\quad N_{s\cup 0}(T):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\\ m_{\rho}=1\ \textup{or}\ \beta=1/2\end{subarray}}1,\quad\textup{ and }\quad N_{d}(T):=\left|\left\{\rho:0<\gamma\leqslant T\right\}\right|.

Thus Ns​(T)N_{s}(T) denotes the number of simple zeros, Nd​(T)N_{d}(T) the number of distinct zeros, and Ns∪0​(T)N_{s\cup 0}(T) the number of zeros that are simple or lie on the critical line, counted with multiplicity, all up to height TT.

In 1973, Montgomery [19] established his pair correlation theorem for the zeros of the zeta function and used it to prove, assuming RH, that at least 2/32/3 of the zeros are simple. Montgomery and Taylor (see [20]) subsequently obtained the larger proportion

(1.1) C0:=32−12​cot⁡(12)=0.6725007​…,C_{0}:=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cot\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=0.6725007\ldots,

and this was improved to 0.67920.6792 by Chirre, Gonçalves, and de Laat [7]. By a different method, Conrey, Ghosh and Gonek [9] proved, assuming RH and the Generalized Lindelöf Hypothesis (GLH), that at least 1927=0.7037​…\frac{19}{27}=0.7037\ldots of the zeta zeros are simple, and that at least 0.84560.8456 of the zeros are distinct. Bui and Heath-Brown [5] subsequently removed GLH from this result and obtained the proportion 19/2719/27 assuming only RH. Unconditionally, Farmer [10] proved that more than 63.95%63.95\% of the zeros are distinct. This was improved by Ki and Lee [17, Theorem 5], who proved that more than 70%70\% of the zeros are distinct.

More recently, substantial progress has been made towards removing the Riemann hypothesis from Montgomery’s pair correlation argument. Aryan [2] obtained an unconditional form of the pair correlation formula for the Fejér kernel and showed that Montgomery’s 2/32/3 bound for simple zeros follows from a zero-density hypothesis. Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh [3] subsequently established an unconditional version of Montgomery’s pair correlation theorem and, under hypotheses weaker than RH, proved that at least 61.7%61.7\% of the zeros are simple. In further work [4], they showed for the first time that the pair correlation method can also give information on the horizontal distribution of the zeros. More precisely, they proved that if for all large TT, all the zeros with T<γ⩽2​TT<\gamma\leqslant 2T satisfy |β−12|<b2​log⁡T,|\beta-\frac{1}{2}|<\frac{b}{2\log T}, then at least 2/32/3 of the zeros are simple and on the critical line when b=0.3185b=0.3185, while for b=0.001b=0.001 the corresponding proportion is at least 0.67250.6725. Goldston and Suriajaya [12, 13] subsequently clarified the mechanism behind these results. Moreover, extending earlier work of Gallagher and Mueller [11], Goldston, Lee, Schettler and Suriajaya [14] showed that Montgomery’s full Pair Correlation Conjecture, without assuming RH, implies that asymptotically 100%100\% of the zeros are simple and on the critical line.

The main purpose of this paper is to give a new and conceptually simpler approach to the breakthrough result recently announced by an internal research version of Claude, developed by Anthropic, and subsequently verified by Alpöge and Furman [1]. In addition to recovering their bounds, our approach yields two further unconditional estimates concerning simple zeros and zeros on the critical line.

Theorem 1.1.

We have

lim infT→∞N0s​(T)N⁡(T)⩾C0=0.67250​…, and lim infT→∞Nd​(T)N⁡(T)⩾C1:=C0+12=0.83625​….\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{0}^{\textup{s}}(T)}{N(T)}\geqslant C_{0}=0.67250\ldots,\quad\textup{ and }\quad\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{d}(T)}{N(T)}\geqslant C_{1}:=\frac{C_{0}+1}{2}=0.83625\ldots.

Moreover, we have

lim infT→∞Ns∪0​(T)N⁡(T)⩾C2=0.88762​…​ and ​lim infT→∞Ns​(T)+N0​(T)2​N​(T)⩾C1=0.83625​….\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{s\cup 0}(T)}{N(T)}\geqslant C_{2}=0.88762\ldots\ \textup{ and }\ \liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{N_{s}(T)+N_{0}(T)}{2N(T)}\geqslant C_{1}=0.83625\ldots.

Here C0C_{0} is defined in (1.1) and C2:=(1+2​2+2​C0)/(3+2​2).C_{2}:=(1+2\sqrt{2}+2C_{0})/(3+2\sqrt{2}). Thus, more than 67.25%67.25\% of the non-trivial zeros of the zeta function are simple and on the critical line, and more than 88.76%88.76\% of the zeros are either simple or lie on the critical line (or both). In addition, more than 83.62%83.62\% of the zeros are distinct, and the average of the proportions of simple zeros and of zeros on the critical line is at least 83.62%83.62\%.

Remark 1.2.

The two additional estimates express a form of “rigidity” between the simplicity and the horizontal location of zeros. The first shows that, asymptotically, the proportion of zeros that are simultaneously off the critical line and of multiplicity at least two is at most 1−C2<0.11241-C_{2}<0.1124. The second shows in particular that if either Ns​(T)/N​(T)N_{s}(T)/N(T) or N0​(T)/N​(T)N_{0}(T)/N(T) tends to the lower bound C0C_{0}, then the other must tend to 11. Note that the last estimate implies that max⁡(N0​(T),Ns​(T))⩾(C1+o⁡(1))​N​(T)\max(N_{0}(T),N_{s}(T))\geqslant(C_{1}+o(1))N(T). Thus, although our argument does not determine which of the two quantities is larger, it shows that the larger of the proportions of zeros on the critical line and of simple zeros is asymptotically at least 83.62%83.62\%. Related estimates are obtained in Theorem 3(ii) and (iii) of Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh [4] through their notion of horizontal multiplicity, under the hypothesis that, for all large TT, all zeros with T<γ⩽2​TT<\gamma\leqslant 2T lie in a narrow box of width b/log⁡Tb/\log T centered on the critical line. In the case b→0b\to 0, their Theorem 3(ii) yields the same lower bound C0+12=C1=0.83625​…\frac{C_{0}+1}{2}=C_{1}=0.83625\ldots for the average of the proportions of simple zeros and of zeros on the critical line. Their Theorem 3(iii), following an observation of Soundararajan, gives under the same assumptions the lower bound 2+C03=0.89083​…\frac{2+C_{0}}{3}=0.89083\ldots for the proportion of zeros that are simple or lie on the critical line (or both), whereas our approach yields the slightly smaller unconditional proportion 0.88762​…0.88762\ldots.

We briefly compare our proof with the argument discovered by Claude and verified by Alpöge and Furman [1]. Their proof starts from Weil’s Hermitian form and restricts it to a finite family of test functions, producing a real symmetric matrix of dimension asymptotic to N⁡(T)N(T). They then evaluate its trace and the sum of the squares of its entries (that is, the square of its Hilbert–Schmidt norm) and combine these estimates with a rank–trace inequality. To this end, they separate the part of the matrix coming from simple zeros on the critical line from the remaining part. The rank–trace inequality then gives a lower bound for the number of simple zeros on the critical line in terms of N⁡(T)N(T), the trace of the matrix, and the square of its Hilbert–Schmidt norm.

Our proof takes a different and more direct route. We avoid the finite-dimensional matrix construction altogether, and replace the linear algebra part of the argument by a single Hilbert space inequality. This reduces the problem directly to an estimate for a pair correlation sum over the zeros, to which we apply Montgomery’s pair correlation theorem in the unconditional form obtained by Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh (see Lemma 5 of [3]). The Hilbert space formulation makes the underlying structure more transparent and allows additional inequalities to be extracted directly.

Although the two proofs are quite different, they both ultimately reduce the relevant information to the estimation of a certain quadratic form over the zeros. In this sense, both may be viewed as variants of a second-moment argument, and the optimization leads in both cases to the same Montgomery–Taylor extremal problem (see Remark 3.4 below), which explains why the same constants appear in the two proofs.

2. The key proposition

Since non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are counted with multiplicity, we will be working with multisets instead of sets of zeros. Montgomery’s classical argument in [19], which shows that at least 2/32/3 of the zeros of the zeta function are simple assuming RH, relies on the following basic inequality

(2.1) ∑ρ0<γ⩽Tmρ=11⩾∑ρ0<γ⩽T(2−mρ)=2​∑ρ0<γ⩽T1−∑ρ,ρ′0<γ,γ′⩽Tρ=ρ′1,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\\ m_{\rho}=1\end{subarray}}1\geqslant\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\end{subarray}}(2-m_{\rho})=2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho\\ 0<\gamma\leqslant T\end{subarray}}1-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho,\rho^{\prime}\\ 0<\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\leqslant T\\ \rho=\rho^{\prime}\end{subarray}}1,

which is true unconditionally. Therefore, one reduces the problem to obtaining an upper bound for the diagonal contribution on the right hand side of (2.1). If RH is assumed then one has

(2.2) ∑ρ,ρ′0<γ,γ′⩽Tρ=ρ′1⩽∑ρ,ρ′0<γ,γ′⩽TK⁡(i⁡(ρ−ρ′)​log⁡T2​π)​44−(ρ−ρ′)2,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho,\rho^{\prime}\\ 0<\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\leqslant T\\ \rho=\rho^{\prime}\end{subarray}}1\leqslant\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho,\rho^{\prime}\\ 0<\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\leqslant T\end{subarray}}K\left(i(\rho-\rho^{\prime})\frac{\log T}{2\pi}\right)\frac{4}{4-(\rho-\rho^{\prime})^{2}},

for any kernel22 2 Since in this case i⁡(ρ−ρ′)=γ′−γ∈ℝi(\rho-\rho^{\prime})=\gamma^{\prime}-\gamma\in\mathbb{R}. KK such that K⁡(0)=1K(0)=1 and K⁡(u)⩾0K(u)\geqslant 0 for all u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}. Assuming RH, Montgomery then computes this pair correlation sum with KK being the Fejér kernel K⁡(u)=(sin⁡(π​u)π​u)2K(u)=\left(\frac{\sin(\pi u)}{\pi u}\right)^{2}. Recent attempts to use this approach unconditionally relied on some form of positivity for KK when evaluated at differences of non-trivial zeros that may lie off the critical line. In [4], Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh achieved this using a kernel of Tsang whose real part is positive in a fixed horizontal strip. After rescaling by log⁡T/(2​π)\log T/(2\pi), this positivity applies only if one assumes that all the non-trivial zeros with imaginary part in [T,2​T][T,2T] lie in a very narrow strip of the form |β−1/2|⩽c/log⁡T|\beta-1/2|\leqslant c/\log T. This restriction cannot be removed merely by searching for a better kernel. Indeed, for the above method to work without any information on the real parts of the zeros, one would require that the kernel KK satisfies Re​K​(z)⩾0\textup{Re}K(z)\geqslant 0 for all z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C}. However, no such nonconstant entire kernel exists.

Our key idea is that one can bypass the inequality (2.1) and directly prove, for a large class of kernels KK, that the number of simple real elements of a finite multiset 𝒵\mathcal{Z} which is invariant under complex conjugation is

⩾2​∑z∈𝒵1−∑z,s∈𝒵K​(z−s)2,\geqslant 2\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}1-\sum_{z,s\in\mathcal{Z}}K(z-s)^{2},

without requiring that the individual off-diagonal terms K​(z−s)2K(z-s)^{2} be non-negative.

Remark 2.2.

There are two reasons for working with K2K^{2}, instead of KK, in Proposition 2.1. Indeed, since the number of simple real elements of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is at most ∑z∈𝒵1\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}1, the inequality (2.4) implies that ∑z,s∈𝒵K​(z−s)2⩾∑z∈𝒵1\sum_{z,s\in\mathcal{Z}}K(z-s)^{2}\geqslant\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}1. 3. Proof of Theorem 1.1

For complex numbers zz with |Re​(z)|<2|\textup{Re}(z)|<2 we define

We shall use the following unconditional pair correlation formula established by Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya and Turnage-Butterbaugh in [3]. Its proof follows the same argument as Montgomery’s original proof under RH [19], while an unconditional form of the special case corresponding to the Fejér kernel was previously obtained by Aryan [2].

Lemma 3.1 (Lemma 5 of [3]).

Let f∈L1​(ℝ)f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) be a real-valued even function with support in [−1,1][-1,1], and suppose that ff is Lipschitz continuous at x=0x=0 (that is, f⁡(x)−f⁡(0)=O⁡(|x|)f(x)-f(0)=O(|x|) as x→0x\to 0). Then we have

To combine Proposition 2.1 with the pair correlation formula in Lemma 3.1, we must remove the weight w⁡(ρ−ρ′)w(\rho-\rho^{\prime}). Indeed, let η∈Cc∞((−1/2,1/2))\eta\in C_{c}^{\infty}((-1/2,1/2)) be a real valued even function such that η2^​(0)=1\widehat{\eta^{2}}(0)=1. for all f,g∈L2​(ℝ)f,g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). Then Q^=K2\widehat{Q}=K^{2} and QQ is supported in [−1,1][-1,1]. Hence a direct application of Lemma 3.1 gives an asymptotic formula for the weighted sum

∑ρ,ρ′0<γ,γ′⩽TK​(i⁡(ρ−ρ′)​log⁡T2​π)2​w​(ρ−ρ′).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\rho,\rho^{\prime}\\ 0<\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\leqslant T\end{subarray}}K\left(i(\rho-\rho^{\prime})\frac{\log T}{2\pi}\right)^{2}w(\rho-\rho^{\prime}).

On the other hand, in order to use Proposition 2.1 we need to estimate the corresponding sum without the factor w⁡(ρ−ρ′)w(\rho-\rho^{\prime}). This factor cannot be removed by directly applying Lemma 3.1 to a different test function. Indeed, writing z=i⁡(ρ−ρ′)​log⁡T2​π,z=i(\rho-\rho^{\prime})\frac{\log T}{2\pi}, we have

Thus, the identity

which depends on TT. Hence, Lemma 3.1 cannot be applied directly to such a test function without an additional uniformity argument. To overcome this we express the desired kernel as a linear combination of two fixed test functions to which Lemma 3.1 can be applied separately.

Appendix A Formal Certificate by AxiomProver

AxiomProver, an AI system currently under development by Axiom Math, autonomously generated (from natural language) an unconditional formal certificate for Proposition 2.1. Using Proposition 2.1, a formal certificate was also autonomously generated for Theorem 1.1 under the assumptions of [3, Lemma 5] (see Lemma 3.1 above) and the standard Riemann–von Mangoldt asymptotic N⁡(T)∼12​π​T​log⁡TN(T)\sim\frac{1}{2\pi}T\log T (see [23, Theorem 9.4]). The certificates can be found in

https://github.com/AxiomMath/ZetaZerosV2

This repository contains a formal challenge file containing the statements of the three main results, which can be mechanically verified using the Comparator tool in Lean.

Instructions for reporting errors
